q: 1. Which of the salt present in water is harmful for cultivation purposes?
explain: Sodium carbonate (Black Alkali) is highly harmful as it reacts with soil to form a hard, impermeable crust and significantly raises soil pH.

q: 2. The whole period of cultivation from the time when irrigation water is first supplied for preparation of the ground to its last watering before harvesting, is called
explain: Base period ($B$) is used in engineering calculations for duty and delta; it is slightly shorter than the crop period.

q: 3. Where steep land is a available, the method of irrigation adopted is
explain: Free flooding (or wild flooding) is used on steep or irregular land where creating borders or checks is not economically feasible.

q: 4. For closed growing crops (such as wheat), the method of irrigation used is
explain: Border flooding is very effective for close-growing crops like wheat or barley because it provides uniform distribution over long strips.

q: 5. Check flooding method of irrigation is used for
options: crops which can stand inundation of water for sometime
crops such as sugarcane, potatoes etc.
explain: Check flooding involves surrounding plots with low levees; it is ideal for heavy soils or crops like rice that can handle standing water.

q: 6. Sprinkler irrigation is adopted for ............. areas.
explain: Sprinkler irrigation is highly versatile for uneven or undulating topography where surface irrigation would require expensive land leveling.

q: 7. The method of irrigation used for orchards is
explain: In basin flooding, a circular or square basin is formed around each tree or group of trees, which is common in orchard management.

q: 8. The earth's water circulatory system, is known as
explain: The hydrologic cycle describes the continuous movement of water on, above, and below the surface of the Earth.

q: 9. The precipitation caused by natural rising of warmer lighter air colder and denser surroundings is called
explain: Convective precipitation occurs when the earth's surface is heated, causing warm air to rise, cool, and condense into rain.

q: 10. A graph showing variations of discharge with time, at a particular point of a stream is known as
explain: A hydrograph plots the river discharge (flow rate) against time, showing how a stream responds to rainfall.

q: 11. A hydrograph representing one cm of runoff from a rainfall of some unit duration and specific area distribution is known as
explain: The unit hydrograph is a fundamental tool in hydrology representing the response of a watershed to 1 cm of effective rainfall.

q: 12. Run-off is measure in
explain: Run-off rate (discharge) is conventionally measured in cubic meters per second (cumecs).

q: 13. Irrigation canals are generally aligned along
explain: Aligning along the watershed (ridge) is preferred because it eliminates the need for expensive cross-drainage works.

q: 14. A land is said to be water-logged when
options: the air circulation is stopped in the root zone due to the rise in water table
the soil pores within a depth of 40 cm are saturated
explain: Waterlogging occurs when the water table rises to the root zone, displacing air and preventing the oxygen circulation necessary for plant growth.

q: 15. The infertility of the soil in water-logged areas is due to
options: inhibiting activity of the soil bacteria
explain: Waterlogging leads to anaerobic conditions (killing aerobic bacteria), salt accumulation (salinization), and the proliferation of water-loving weeds.

q: 16. Water logging is caused due to
explain: It is generally caused by a combination of excessive water input (rain/irrigation) and the inability of that water to drain away naturally or artificially.

q: 17. The soil becomes, practically, infertile if its pH value is
explain: A pH of 11 indicates highly alkaline (sodic) soil, which is toxic to most crops and destroys soil structure.

q: 18. The measure adopted to reclaim the water-logged area is
explain: Reclamation involves reducing water input (lining) and removing excess groundwater (lift irrigation/pumping) or adjusting canal levels.

q: 19. Rivers on alluvial plains may be .............
explain: Alluvial rivers are dynamic; they can meander (looping), aggrade (deposit sediment), or degrade (scour the bed) depending on silt load and discharge.

q: 20. A river meandering through an alluvial plain has a series of consecutive reversed order connected with short straight sketches, is called .............
explain: A 'crossing' is the relatively short, straight reach of a river between two consecutive reverse bends (meanders).

q: 21. The tortuosity of a meandering river is always ............. one.
explain: Tortuosity is the ratio of the actual curved length along the river channel to the direct axial distance. Since the curve is always longer, the ratio is > 1.

q: 22. The basic factor which controls the process of meandering is .............
explain: Meandering is a complex morphological process influenced by the energy of the water (discharge/slope) and the erodibility of the banks.

q: 23. When river flows in a plain country, its stage is known as ............. stage.
explain: The 'trough' or 'alluvial' stage occurs when the river reaches the plains, characterized by a bed of sand and silt rather than boulders.

q: 24. The width and length of meander as well as width of river, vary approximately with .............
explain: According to regime theories (Lacey/Inglis), meander parameters like width and length are generally proportional to $\sqrt{Q}$ (square root of discharge).

q: 25. The method used for training of rivers is .............
explain: River training involves various structures: Guide banks (flow direction), Levees (flood protection), and Groynes (bank protection/channel narrowing).

q: 26. A river training work is generally required when the river is .............
explain: Meandering rivers are unstable and prone to bank erosion and shifting courses, making training works essential to protect infrastructure.

options: contracts a river channel to improve its depth
silts up the area in the vicinity by creating a slack flow
trains the flow along a certain course
explain: Groynes serve multiple purposes including protecting banks, narrowing the channel for navigation, and encouraging silting in undesired scour zones.

q: 28. A deflecting groyne has a much ............. length than a repelling groyne.
explain: Deflecting groynes are short and only change the local flow direction, whereas repelling groynes are longer and designed to push the main current away.

q: 29. A deflecting groyne in a river is .............
explain: Deflecting groynes are typically inclined downstream (pointing with the flow) to nudge the current away from the bank.

q: 30. A levee on flood .............
options: increases the water surface elevation of the river at flood
decreases the surface slope of the stream above the leveed portion
increases the velocity and scouring action through leveed section
explain: Levees confine floodwaters, which naturally raises the water level, increases velocity due to lack of lateral spread, and changes the energy gradient.

q: 31. A groyne with a curved head is known as .............
explain: A Burma-type groyne is specifically characterized by having a curved or T-shaped head to provide better flow stabilization at the tip.

q: 32. A water-logged land is found suitable for cultivation due to .............
options: regular supply of water by capillary action
explain: Waterlogged land is actually unsuitable for most cultivation because the lack of air in the soil 'suffocates' plant roots.

q: 33. The top of the capillary zone .............
options: lies below the water table at every point
lies above the water table at every point
coincides the water table at every point
explain: Capillary action pulls water upward against gravity, so the capillary fringe always sits immediately above the phreatic surface (water table).

q: 34. The measure to remove water logging of land, is .............
options: to increase outflow from the ground water reservoir
explain: Remediation involves both prevention (lining canals to stop seepage) and drainage (pumping or surface drains to lower the water table).

q: 35. A hydraulic structure is designed to withstand .............
explain: Structural integrity requires accounting for static water pressure, the dynamic energy of jumps, and the subsurface forces from seepage (uplift).

q: 36. The water face of the guide banks, is protected by .............
explain: The term 'one-man stone' refers to stones that can be handled by one person, commonly used for pitching guide banks to prevent erosion.

q: 37. Attracting groynes are built .............
explain: Attracting groynes point downstream; this orientation 'invites' the current toward the bank they are attached to, usually to move the channel away from the opposite bank.
